Mathematically, there will always be some level of inequality where this is true, almost independent of tax levels or tax structure. America could have one low flat tax, and there would still be some level of inequality where this is true.

This is because basic expenses are relatively fixed across Americans compared to financial inequality between Americans. A sufficiently rich person could buy every home on your block, and still be spending a significantly smaller portion of their income on housing than you are. Yet even with a flat tax, they would be guaranteed to spend the same portion of their income on taxes as you are.

There are natural limitations that prevent rich people from owning more than 10,000 times as much housing than you, or eating more than 10,000 times as much food as you. But inequality keeps growing without bound. Maybe you're fine with that - I'm not making a values statement here. I'm just saying that it makes this mathematical outcome inevitable, independent of tax levels.

One evening President McKinley was having a hard time deciding which of two equally competent men to appoint to an important diplomatic post. Suddenly he recalled an incident that had occurred on a stormy night many years before. He had boarded a streetcar and taken the last empty seat at the rear. At one point an old washer-woman carrying a heavy basket boarded the car, and stood forlorn in the aisle.

One of the men whom McKinley was now considering for the post had been sitting right in front of the old lady, but shifted his newspaper in such a way as to seem not to see her. McKinley went down the aisle, picked up the basket of washing, and led the old lady back to his seat. The man with the newspaper, looking down, did not see this.

"The candidate never knew," said McKinley's friend Charles G. Dawes, who reported the story, "this little act of selfishness, or rather this little omission of kindness, had deprived him of that which would have crowned his ambition of a lifetime."

Source:

Boller, Paul F. "William B. McKinley" Presidential Anecdotes. New York: Oxford UP, 1981. 192. Print.

i doubt the veracity of this story. i don't doubt it is a quote, i just doubt the person speaking told the truth. there are many justifications for actions and human long term memory is not like a camera, it is warped with current mood/circumstance/environment. if it was a choice between person A and person B and person A was overlooked, than it is likely caused by favoritism towards person B and justification for emotional decision afterwards (the story about the seat).

understanding how your thoughts works gives you more autonomy. i encourage people to go look at modern neuropsychology to see how decision making really works as opposed to how we perceive it to work. also i encourage people to go check out different types of illusions. it is a good way to show you first hand that your senses can and do lie to you all the time, and that your perception is an illusion of sorts. memory is a cognitive illusion, it may be mostly accurate but it is missing details.

While I agree with everything you said, I also feel like everyone is different.

What I mean by that, is that no one should ever assume that everyone else's thought processes work the same. Saying "most people think the same" is fine, but not all people.

For example, people often debate about whether sexuality is a choice. I'm of the opinion that it is for some and not for others, and for each of them, the reason why it's not a choice is probably different.

And I personally don't think pure scientific testing will ever make true headway in terms of understand our own minds. Not as in physicaly, i.e. this part of the brain does <thing>, but as in, consciously, i.e. you thought or chose to do this for <reason>. Simply because, if we are all the same, then it should make headway (and it appears to not have to me), and if we are not all the same, we can't test for it because the test results come from humans.

And as you said, "it is a good way to show you first hand that your senses can and do lie to you all the time, and that your perception is an illusion of sorts" So if we get our information from human actions based on these senses, and there is no control other than other human senses, how do you discern the static from the noise?

I don't think we can until we get a computer interface into the brain. Then we just record data for a while and start looking for patterns.

But I'm no ... well, anything related to brain science or statistics.
